narrative:
FIRST WARN FORECAST
Saturday, September 5, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

EXTREME HEAT CONTINUES TODAY, COOLER AIR ARRIVES SUNDAY AND MONDAY

The prolonged late-summer heatwave reaches its final dangerous peak today before a noticeable change in the weather pattern brings cooler and less humid conditions for Sunday and especially Labor Day. Saturday will remain dangerously hot, with afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid-90s to around 100 degrees and heat index values reaching approximately 105 to 110 degrees across portions of the region.

A few isolated showers and thunderstorms will be possible this afternoon and evening, particularly across southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois. However, coverage will remain limited, and most locations will stay dry. The more important weather story today is the heat, not the rain.

The pattern begins to change tonight as a backdoor cold front moves southwestward through the region. This will mark the beginning of a much-needed break from the extreme heat, although temperatures will remain above average through much of the Labor Day weekend.

SATURDAY: ANOTHER DANGEROUSLY HOT DAY

The upper-level ridge responsible for nearly a week of excessive heat is finally beginning to lose its grip on the Mid-Mississippi River Valley. However, that change will come too late to prevent another very hot day across the region.

Temperatures will again reach the mid-90s to around 100 degrees, with the highest readings possible across parts of Missouri and Illinois. Increasing moisture ahead of the approaching front will result in higher dewpoints, which means the heat will feel even more oppressive than the thermometer suggests.

Heat index values are expected to reach 105 to 110 degrees in many areas. These conditions can become dangerous quickly, particularly for anyone spending extended periods outdoors, working in the heat, exercising, or without reliable air conditioning.

This will be the final day of the current stretch of extreme heat, but it should be treated seriously.

ISOLATED STORMS THIS AFTERNOON

The approaching front and increasing atmospheric instability will provide a better opportunity for isolated showers and thunderstorms this afternoon and evening.

The greatest chance for development will be across southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois, with a few additional showers or storms possible elsewhere. Most locations will remain dry.

Atmospheric instability will be sufficient for a few storms to become briefly strong, and an isolated microburst or damaging wind gust cannot be ruled out. However, limited wind shear should prevent widespread severe weather, and most storms will be short-lived.

Any showers and thunderstorms that develop should diminish rapidly this evening as daytime heating fades.

SUNDAY: THE HEAT FINALLY BEGINS TO BREAK

The backdoor cold front will move completely through the region by Sunday, bringing a significant change in temperatures and humidity.

Sunday will still be warmer than average for early September, with temperatures generally ranging from the mid-80s to lower 90s. The warmest conditions are expected across central and southeastern Missouri, where higher humidity will linger behind the front.

There remains some potential for heat index values to reach 100 degrees in those areas, but confidence in widespread excessive heat has decreased. At this time, additional heat headlines do not appear necessary for most of the region.

A stray shower or thunderstorm could clip portions of northeastern or central Missouri Sunday afternoon or evening, but the overwhelming majority of the area should remain dry.

LABOR DAY: A MUCH-NEEDED BREAK

Monday will bring the most noticeable improvement in the weather.

High pressure will build into the region while significantly drier air filters southward. Afternoon temperatures should range from the mid-80s to around 90 degrees, with considerably lower humidity.

Dewpoints will fall into the 60s, with some locations along and east of the Mississippi River potentially seeing dewpoints in the 50s Monday afternoon. That will make a substantial difference compared with the oppressive humidity experienced this week.

While temperatures will still run somewhat above average for early September, Monday should feel dramatically more comfortable.

For the first time in several days, outdoor plans should be much more manageable.

THE HEAT RETURNS TUESDAY

Unfortunately, the cooler weather will be short-lived.

The upper-level ridge will begin shifting eastward again Tuesday, allowing warmer air to return from the southwest. Temperatures will once again climb into the mid-90s to around 100 degrees Tuesday and Wednesday.

There is one important difference compared with the current heatwave. The next warmup is expected to be much shorter.

Moisture will take longer to return Tuesday, meaning heat index values should remain relatively close to actual air temperatures. This could keep Tuesday from becoming as oppressive as Saturday.

By Wednesday, increasing moisture near an approaching cold front could push heat index values higher. However, clouds, showers, thunderstorms, and the timing of the front will make Wednesday's temperatures considerably more uncertain.

At this point, it is too early to determine whether additional heat headlines will be required.

A MORE ACTIVE WEATHER PATTERN DEVELOPS LATE NEXT WEEK

The weather pattern becomes increasingly unsettled from late Wednesday into the second half of next week.

A series of upper-level disturbances will gradually weaken and flatten the ridge that has dominated our weather pattern. The cold front moving through Wednesday may stall or progress southward only slowly, creating a boundary between warmer air to the south and more seasonable air to the north.

That boundary could become a focus for periodic showers and thunderstorms.

Rain chances from Wednesday onward remain uncertain, but ensemble guidance suggests precipitation probabilities generally ranging from 30 to 60 percent at various times. The exact location of the front will be critical to determining who sees rain and who remains dry.

Temperatures also become more difficult to forecast late next week. Current guidance generally favors readings in the 80s to around 90 degrees Thursday and Friday, although considerable variation remains possible depending on the position of the front.

HEAT SAFETY

Today is another day to take the heat seriously.

Drink plenty of water, limit strenuous outdoor activity during the hottest part of the afternoon, take frequent breaks in air conditioning or shade, and never leave children or pets unattended in a vehicle.

Remember that heat illness can develop quickly. If you experience dizziness, confusion, severe headache, nausea, weakness, or other signs of heat-related illness, move to a cooler location and seek medical attention when necessary.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Saturday will be the final and potentially most dangerous day of this extended heatwave, with temperatures in the mid-90s to around 100 degrees and heat index values reaching 105 to 110 degrees.

A few isolated thunderstorms are possible this afternoon and evening, but most locations will remain dry.

A backdoor cold front will bring a welcome change beginning Sunday. Temperatures will fall into the 80s and lower 90s Sunday, followed by an even more comfortable Labor Day with lower humidity and temperatures primarily in the mid-80s to around 90 degrees.

The break will be brief. Heat returns Tuesday and Wednesday, but the next warmup appears likely to be considerably shorter than the prolonged heatwave we are leaving behind.

By late next week, a more active pattern may develop as the ridge weakens and a frontal boundary settles across the region. That could finally provide a more sustained transition toward typical September weather.

Meteorological fall has arrived, but summer has certainly made it clear that it is not ready to leave quietly.
severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

🔴 Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5)

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Northeast Missouri
Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
